This project tests whether LAPD's shift from PredPol to DICFP corresponds to a measurable change in enforcement intensity, and whether any such change is uniform across neighborhoods or concentrated by racial composition. The analysis compares tract-level arrest-to-crime ratios across the PredPol and DICFP eras, then tests whether the size of that change depends on a tract's Black/Latino population share.

Dependent variable: count of arrests per tract-period, modeled as a rate relative to reported crime (see below). Enforcement intensity is the underlying construct. Tracts where arrests exceed what reported crime would predict.

Independent variable: policing-era period. The PredPol era (2016-2019) is compared against the DICFP era (2022-2024), with 2020-2021 dropped to isolate COVID-era confounds from the program change itself. 2015 belongs to the PredPol era but is excluded because four LAPD divisions are missing from that year's crime records while their arrest records are complete (see Data).

Unit of analysis: census tract, matched to ACS demographic data, with LAPD division as a fallback if tract-level crime/arrest data proves too sparse. Three groups of tracts are set aside before estimation. Tracts numbered in the 9800s are Census special land use, covering airports, ports, parks, and large institutions; they record incidents but house almost no residents, so a population share computed over a handful of people is not a measurement of neighborhood composition. `r n_dropped_zero_crime` tract-periods report no crime at all, which leaves the rate undefined. A further `r n_dropped_no_demographics` have no ACS composition estimate. That leaves `r n_tract_periods` tract-periods, and every count reported below describes that estimation sample rather than the larger table it is drawn from.

Moderating variable: tract racial composition, measured as the combined share of residents who are non-Hispanic Black or Hispanic/Latino of any race, from ACS table B03002. The two groups are combined rather than entered separately, and the reason is a limitation of the categories rather than a claim that the groups are interchangeable. Census race and Hispanic origin are asked as separate questions, so "Black" in the tabulated categories means Black alone and not Hispanic, which excludes both Afro-Latino residents and anyone who reports Black together with another race. Across the tracts analyzed here, 15.9% of residents fall in a "two or more races" category, and 23.7% are Hispanic residents reporting "some other race alone," a response pattern common where respondents do not identify with the available race categories. Measuring Black residents as Black alone and not Hispanic counts 408,559 people; measuring them as Black alone or in combination with another race counts 507,659, a difference of roughly 99,000 residents, or 24%. A specification that separates the two groups therefore assigns multiracial residents to one bucket, the other, or neither, and the resulting coefficients are sensitive to a coding decision with no principled answer. The combined measure is stable under that ambiguity, because a resident who is Black, Latino, or both falls inside it in every coding. What it gives up is the ability to attribute a change to one group rather than the other, which is taken up in the Discussion.

To test whether the pre/post decline in enforcement intensity is uniform across neighborhoods or concentrated in majority-Black/Latino tracts, period is interacted with tract racial composition. Rather than model the arrest-to-crime ratio directly, arrest counts are modeled as a negative binomial rate with reported crime entered as an offset:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Arrests}_{it} &\sim \text{NegBinomial}(\mu_{it}, \theta) \\
\log(\mu_{it}) &= \log(\text{Crime}_{it}) + \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Period}_t \\
&\quad + \beta_2 \text{PctBlackLatino}_i + \beta_3 (\text{Period}_t \times \text{PctBlackLatino}_i)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $i$ indexes census tract and $t$ indexes era (PredPol vs. DICFP). Fixing the coefficient on $\log(\text{Crime}_{it})$ at 1 (the offset) is what turns this into a model of the arrest *rate* relative to crime rather than of arrest counts in isolation. $\beta_3$ is the coefficient of interest: it tests whether the DICFP-era change in enforcement intensity differs by tract racial composition.

Modeling arrest counts directly, rather than the arrest-to-crime ratio, is the appropriate specification for two reasons: it handles zero-arrest tract-periods natively, and it lets the ratio's precision scale with the underlying crime volume instead of treating every computed ratio as equally informative.

A small but non-trivial share of tract-periods (`r n_zero_arrest` of `r n_tract_periods`, about `r pct_zero_arrest`) have zero arrests. These are valid observations of low enforcement intensity and should not be dropped. A ratio-based approach handles them unevenly. The arrest-to-crime ratio is undefined for tracts with zero reported crime, which is already excluded from the sample; separately, a log transform of the ratio is undefined at zero arrests, which would force dropping or artificially adjusting exactly those tract-periods. Modeling arrest counts directly with a log link and a crime offset, rather than dividing by crime first, keeps zero-arrest tract-periods in the analysis and avoids ever taking a log of zero.

Even where the ratio is well-defined, computing it by hand and feeding it to OLS treats a ratio of 0 from 1 crime and 0 arrests the same as a ratio of 0 from 500 crimes and 0 arrests, even though the latter is far stronger evidence of low enforcement intensity. A count model with a crime offset does not have this problem: the ratio interpretation falls out of the offset, and the model's own variance structure naturally gives more weight to tract-periods with more underlying crime.

Negative binomial, rather than Poisson, is used because arrest counts are heavily overdispersed: the raw variance-to-mean ratio in the data is approximately `r dispersion_ratio`, far past the equidispersion that Poisson assumes. This mirrors standard practice in the neighborhood crime-count literature; @semenza-etal_2022_eviction-crime-neighborhood, studying homicide, robbery, and burglary counts across Philadelphia census tracts, likewise treat overdispersion as a given for neighborhood-level crime counts and fit negative binomial models directly rather than starting from Poisson and testing.

Each tract in this design contributes one observation per era, so the two observations from the same tract are not independent. Following the same precedent, the model is estimated as a population-averaged negative binomial GEE (generalized estimating equations) model clustered by tract, rather than a standard GLM with cluster-robust standard errors added afterward. A GEE directly models the within-tract correlation structure across periods rather than treating it as a correction applied after the fact, and, per @semenza-etal_2022_eviction-crime-neighborhood, is more robust to misspecification of that correlation structure than fixed- or random-effects panel alternatives. See Data for the R implementation.
